Design
 Instrument Junction Box: 9 Smart Rules for Safe Wiring
 Every field transmitter, switch and valve signal passes through a junction box before it reaches the control room. A well designed box keeps those signals safe, dry, segregated and easy to trace for the whole life of the plant.
 Single and Multi Pair 
 Terminal Sizing 
 IS Segregation 
 Ex e and Ex d 
 A junction box looks like a simple steel enclosure, yet poor design causes water ingress, noise, wrong wiring and hazardous area failures. This guide covers the practical rules for designing and specifying one correctly.
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how an instrument junction box is designed, from terminal sizing and spares to IS segregation, Ex protection, IP rating, glands and the JB schedule.
 What Is an Instrument Junction Box?
 An instrument junction box is a field enclosure where the individual cables from several instruments are terminated and joined to one multicore cable that runs to the control room. It reduces the number of long cables, keeps terminations protected and gives a convenient point for testing and fault finding.
 In a typical plant, the field JB sits between the instruments and the marshalling cabinet . From there the signals go to the DCS, PLC or safety system input cards.
 Image credit: Control and Instrumentation . Photo courtesy of Control and Instrumentation, shown here for educational reference. 
 The same box idea is used for analog loops, digital signals, thermocouples, fieldbus spurs and power to solenoids. How the cables are routed from the field to the system is shown in PLC wiring from field instrument to system cabinet .
 Advertisement 
 Single Pair and Multi Pair Instrument Junction Box Types
 Single Pair JB
 Terminates one instrument cable, often for a splice or a remote device.
 Best for: long runs, isolated instruments
 Simple 
 Multi Pair JB
 Collects 6 to 48 or more field pairs onto one or two multicore cables.
 Best for: process units with many instruments
 Most Common 
 Fieldbus or Power JB
 Holds device couplers, spur protection or solenoid power terminals.
 Best for: Foundation Fieldbus, Profibus PA, valve power
 Special 
 Each multicore pair carries one loop, such as a 4 to 20 mA current loop , with an overall shield and often an individual shield per pair. Thermocouple extension cables need their own JB with compensating terminals.
 Do You Know?
 Many specifications ask for multicore cables with two or more unused pairs left for future use. Control and Instrumentation recommends this so new instruments can be added without pulling a new cable.
 9 Design Rules for an Instrument Junction Box
 1
 Group by Signal
 Keep analog, digital, power and fieldbus in separate boxes.
 2
 Segregate IS
 Never mix IS and non IS circuits in the same box without approved separation.
 3
 Match the Area
 Select Ex e, Ex d or Ex i suitable for the zone, gas group and T class.
 4
 Pick IP Rating
 Use IP56 or better outdoors, higher for washdown.
 5
 Choose Material
 SS316L or GRP for outdoor and corrosive sites.
 6
 Size Terminals
 Allow for all cores, shields and the spare margin.
 7
 Plan Entries
 Bottom entry glands, certified and with plugs on unused holes.
 8
 Earth Properly
 Provide earth studs and isolated shield bars.
 9
 Label Clearly
 Tag the box, terminals and cores to match the JB schedule.
 Quick Tip
 Mount the box so that all glands enter from the bottom. Top entry glands collect rainwater and are the most common cause of water inside a JB.
 Terminal Sizing and Spare Philosophy
 When sizing an instrument junction box, count the terminals for every core, then add separate terminals for each pair shield and the overall shield. A 3 wire RTD or a 4 wire loop needs more terminals than a 2 wire transmitter, so read the instrument list carefully.
 Most projects keep about 10 to 20 percent spare terminals and spare multicore pairs, as specified by the client. Spare cores should be terminated on spare terminals and labelled, not left loose inside the box.
 Used terminals = Instruments × Terminals per loop 
 Spare terminals = Used terminals × Spare % ÷ 100 
 Multicore pairs ≥ Instruments × (1 + Spare % ÷ 100) 
Example:
20 transmitters, 3 terminals each (plus, minus, shield), 20 percent spare
Used = 20 × 3 = 60, spare = 60 × 20 ÷ 100 = 12
 Total terminals = 72, multicore pairs at least 24 
 Choose terminals rated for the conductor size, usually 1.5 or 2.5 square mm for signals. Disconnect or knife terminals on loops help testing without lifting wires, and fused terminals suit solenoid power.

 Second Worked Example: Mixed Signal Area
 A compressor skid has 14 transmitters with 3 terminals each and 6 RTDs with 4 terminals each, and the client wants 15 percent spare. Used terminals are 14 × 3 plus 6 × 4, which is 66, and the spare is 66 × 0.15, rounded up to 10.
 The box therefore needs at least 76 signal terminals, plus end stops, earth bar and markers. The multicore needs at least 20 × 1.15, rounded up to 23 pairs, so the next standard 24 pair cable is chosen.
 Advertisement 
 IS and Non IS Segregation Inside the JB
 Intrinsically safe circuits must stay separate from non IS wiring, as explained in explosion proof vs intrinsically safe instruments . The simplest and preferred way is a dedicated IS instrument junction box with only IS circuits inside.
 IEC 60079 14 requires a clearance of at least 50 mm between IS and non IS terminals when they share a box, or an earthed metal or insulating partition. IS terminals and cables are normally coloured light blue so they are easy to identify.
 Control and Instrumentation notes that boxes holding IS circuits are labelled on the outside, blue with white lettering, stating Intrinsically Safe Circuits. This warns electricians not to connect any other circuit or test equipment that is not IS approved.
 Do You Know?
 An Ex e increased safety box can hold IS circuits as well, but the IS terminals still need the same segregation and blue identification. The Ex e rating does not make the IS circuit any safer by itself.
 Ex e, Ex d and Hazardous Area Choices
 In a classified area, the instrument junction box must suit the zone from the hazardous area classification , the gas group and the temperature class. The ABS guidance note asks for Gas Group II and temperature class T3 as a minimum for offshore junction boxes.
 Protection How It Protects Gland Entry Typical Use 
 Ex e increased safety No sparks, controlled terminals and creepage Bolted gland plate, Ex e glands Most instrument JBs in Zone 1 and 2 
 Ex d flameproof Contains an internal explosion Threaded entries, Ex d glands and plugs Boxes with sparking parts or power 
 Ex i intrinsic safety Limits energy in the circuit Normal IP rated glands IS loops, blue labelled 
 Non Ex industrial No hazardous area protection Industrial glands Safe areas only 
 Ex e boxes are lighter and easier to wire, so they are the usual choice for instrument signals. For certification, the box needs ATEX or IECEx marking, compared in difference between ATEX and IECEx .
 IP Rating, Material and Cable Glands
 Control and Instrumentation states that IP56 is usually the minimum for junction boxes, especially outdoors. The ABS note lists IP21 for indoor rooms with HVAC, IP44 for machinery spaces, IP54 with water mist and IP56 outdoors, as described in IP rating explained .
 SS316L is the preferred material in coastal and offshore plants because it resists chloride corrosion, while GRP suits chemical areas and is light. ABS recommends SS316L gland plates with nickel plated brass glands for offshore boxes.
 Glands must carry the same Ex certification and IP rating as the instrument junction box, and unused entries need certified stopping plugs. Armoured cables need glands that clamp and earth the armour, as covered in cable gland types and selection .
 IP56 Minimum outdoor rating 
 SS316L Preferred offshore material 
 T3 Minimum T class, ABS note 
 M6 to M10 Earth stud sizes 
 Quick Tip
 Fit a breather drain at the lowest point of a large outdoor box. It lets condensation escape without letting rain in, which keeps terminals dry during the monsoon.
 Earthing and Shield Termination
 The instrument junction box body needs an external earth stud, and the ABS note recommends M6 to M10 SS316L studs welded to the enclosure so the IP rating is not lost. The protective earth follows the plant earthing scheme .
 Cable shields are landed on an isolated instrument earth bar, not on the box body, and are earthed at one end only, usually the control room. This avoids the circulating currents described in ground loop causes and prevention .
 Myth: A shield should be earthed at both ends for safety.
 Fact: Signal shields are earthed at one point to avoid ground loops and noise.
 Myth: Any outdoor box with a gasket is good enough.
 Fact: The IP rating must be certified and the glands must match it.
 Myth: IS and non IS wires can share a box freely.
 Fact: They need 50 mm clearance or a partition, and dedicated IS boxes are preferred.
 Myth: Spare terminals waste money.
 Fact: Spares save a costly new cable when instruments are added later.
 Labelling and the JB Schedule
 Each instrument junction box carries a tag plate with its JB number, area and protection marking, and every terminal and core gets a ferrule matching the drawings. Good labels make loop checks and later maintenance far faster.
 The JB schedule lists every instrument tag, field cable, terminal number, multicore cable and pair number for each box. It is the key document used during the instrument loop checking procedure at commissioning.
 Use the plant colour code for cores and shields, following the practice in cable colour codes for field instruments . Keep the schedule updated after every modification so the as built records stay true.
 Box tag, area classification and Ex marking verified
 IP rating and material match the specification
 All glands certified, tight and unused entries plugged
 IS and non IS circuits segregated and blue labelled
 Terminals, ferrules and cores match the JB schedule
 Spare terminals and pairs terminated and labelled
 Shields on isolated bar, earth stud connected
 Insulation resistance and continuity tests recorded
 Instrument Junction Box Installation and Testing
 Mount the instrument junction box on a rigid stand at a convenient working height, away from heat sources and vibration, with clear access for the door. Route cables neatly on trays sized with the cable tray fill calculation .
 Before energising, carry out continuity and insulation resistance tests on every pair. Follow this with the loop check from the field device to the control system screen.
 Advantages of a Well Designed JB
 Fewer long cables and lower installation cost.
 Easy testing and fault finding at one point.
 Safe segregation of IS and non IS circuits.
 Room for future instruments through spares.
 Limitations and Risks
 Extra connection points that can loosen.
 Water ingress if glands or gaskets fail.
 Needs certified parts in hazardous areas.
 Poor labelling makes troubleshooting slow.
 Advertisement 
 Where Field JBs Are Used
 Process Units
 Transmitters and valves grouped by area in refineries and chemical plants.
 Fire and Gas Systems
 Detectors wired through dedicated F and G boxes.
 Compressor and Pump Skids
 Skid edge boxes for vendor packages.
 Tank Farms
 Level, temperature and valve signals collected near the tanks.
 Power Plants
 Boiler and turbine field signals.
 For safety related loops, many owners keep separate boxes for the fire and gas system and the shutdown system. Noise sensitive loops also benefit from shielded twisted pair cable through the box.

 Instrument Junction Box FAQ
 What is an instrument junction box?
 It is a field enclosure where cables from several instruments are terminated and joined to a multicore cable. The multicore then carries all those signals to the control room.
 It reduces cable cost and gives a safe point for testing and fault finding. Each box is tagged and recorded in the JB schedule for traceability.
 How many spare terminals should an instrument junction box have?
 Most projects keep about 10 to 20 percent spare terminals, as specified by the client standard. Spare multicore pairs are also left so future instruments can be added without a new cable.
 Spare cores should be terminated on spare terminals and labelled clearly at both ends. Loose spare cores inside the box can touch live terminals and cause faults.
 Can IS and non IS circuits share one box?
 It is possible only with at least 50 mm clearance or an approved partition between the terminals. Even then, the IS terminals and wiring must be clearly identified in light blue.
 Most designers prefer a dedicated IS box to avoid any mistakes during later work. That box is labelled on the outside as containing intrinsically safe circuits.
 What is the difference between Ex e and Ex d boxes?
 An Ex e box prevents sparks and hot spots through controlled terminals, creepage distances and good sealing. It is light and easy to wire, so it suits most instrument signals
